lessons.title: When I was a child
lessons.goal: Describe what your life used to be like.

tip.title: The imparfait paints the background
tip.body: To say how things used to be — habits, descriptions, feelings — French uses the imparfait: Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à la campagne (When I was little, I lived in the countryside). English often says 'used to' or 'would': Le dimanche, on allait chez ma grand-mère (On Sundays we used to go to my grandmother's). The endings -ais, -ait and -aient all sound the same, 'è': j'habitais, il habitait, ils habitaient. In speech, quand j'étais has a liaison: quan-t-étais.

lessons.title: Telling an anecdote
lessons.goal: Tell a short story with a clear order of events.

tip.title: Setting the scene, then the action
tip.body: A French anecdote mixes two past tenses. The imparfait sets the scene (Il faisait beau, j'étais à la plage), the passé composé moves the story forward (Tout à coup, j'ai vu…). Signal words help your listener: un jour, ce jour-là, d'abord, ensuite, tout à coup, finalement. Pronunciation: tout à coup has a liaison — tou-ta-kou — and the p in coup is silent.

lessons.title: Then and now
lessons.goal: Share memories and say how things have changed.

tip.title: avant / maintenant and something you miss
tip.body: Contrast the past and the present with avant (before, it used to be) + imparfait and maintenant + present: Avant, il y avait une boulangerie ici ; maintenant, c'est une banque. To say you miss something, French turns the sentence around: the thing you miss is the subject of manquer — Mon village me manque (I miss my village), literally 'my village is lacking to me'. Se souvenir de and se rappeler both mean to remember.

lessons.title: Imparfait vs passé composé
lessons.goal: Form the imparfait and choose between it and the passé composé.

tip.title: Background vs event
tip.body: Form the imparfait from the nous form of the present: drop -ons and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient (nous finissons → je finissais, nous faisons → je faisais). The only irregular stem is être: j'étais. Use the imparfait for habits (Le samedi, je jouais au tennis), descriptions (Il faisait froid) and actions in progress (Je lisais…). Use the passé composé for single, completed events (… quand le téléphone a sonné). A handy test: if English could say 'was …-ing' or 'used to', it's the imparfait. Watch the sound: je parlais (è) vs j'ai parlé (é).

story.intro: Léa asks her grandfather, who grew up near Namur in Belgium, what school was like when he was a boy.

lines.n: Oh, it was very different! I lived on the farm and I walked three kilometres every morning.

culture.title: School days and colonies de vacances
culture.body: French pupils are usually marked out of 20, and a 12 or 14 is a respectable grade. In many French primary schools, Wednesday has long been a day off, or at least a free afternoon, which is why so many people remember Wednesdays at their grandparents'. In summer, generations of French children went to a colonie de vacances, or colo — a holiday camp run by young animateurs, often students who hold the BAFA certificate. In Belgium, youth movements such as the scouts organise popular summer camps, and in Québec children go to a camp de jour or a camp de vacances.
